intro: Mirano is a small town on the Venetian mainland, about twenty kilometres west of Venice, where the old families of the lagoon built their country villas and parks. In one of those parks grows a southern magnolia that Italy's national register of monumental trees lists at 378 centimetres round and 20.5 metres tall. A reader stood at its foot with arms spread wide and sent us the photograph.

trees.story:
"Magnolia di Villa Belvedere," the reader called this tree when they sent it to us from Mirano, a small town on the mainland west of Venice, and their photograph makes the case better than any name. They stand at the foot of the trunk with their arms flung wide, and the trunk is still wider.

It is a southern magnolia, Magnolia grandiflora, the evergreen of the American South and a long favourite of Italian villa gardens. Most stay neat. This one has grown into a giant, with a short grey trunk, knotted and scaled, that breaks low into a dozen limbs snaking out in every direction, each one thick as a tree, under a roof of glossy dark leaves. Its old leaves lie in a brown carpet all around.

Italy's national register of monumental trees lists a southern magnolia a few steps from the reader's pin, at Villa Morosini on Via Luigi Mariutto, 378 centimetres round and 20.5 metres tall. The reader gives the same girth, and puts the tree at about 155 years old.

Walk in under the crown, as the reader did, and look up through the limbs.

trees.access: In the villa park in Mirano, where the reader walked up to the trunk. Check the park's opening hours before you go.

question_context: A reader sent us this southern magnolia from Mirano, a town on the Venetian mainland about twenty kilometres west of Venice, and named it after Villa Belvedere. Their photograph shows them standing at the foot of the trunk with their arms spread wide, and the trunk is wider still. The tree is a Magnolia grandiflora, the evergreen magnolia of the American South, a long favourite of Italian villa gardens. This one has a short, knotted grey trunk that breaks low into a dozen thick limbs reaching out in every direction under a dense roof of glossy leaves. Italy's national register of monumental trees lists a southern magnolia a few steps from the reader's pin, at Villa Morosini on Via Luigi Mariutto, 378 centimetres round and 20.5 metres tall. The reader gives the same girth and puts the tree at about 155 years old, a figure that is theirs, not the register's. The pin marks the area the reader placed by hand on the map, so look for the biggest magnolia on the lawn when you get there.
